title: Mirabel and the Horizon
premise: Beatrix Fairweather, a xenolinguist who lost her ability to dream in human languages after decades of translating for the dying colony worlds, runs the long route between worlds that no longer speak, ferrying messages for a war she refuses to take sides in. When the colony's children begin sharing one identical dream — a dream written in a language only Beatrix can half-read — she realizes it is a message from the silenced alien civilization both governments claim is extinct. Hunted by her former employer, torn between her duty to the fleet that made her and her love for the colony doctor who treats the dream-sick children, Beatrix must choose whether to deliver the message that will end the war or bury it and keep everyone she loves safe. In the end she broadcasts it from the horizon relay itself, at the cost of her own translation gift, and the war ends not with surrender but with the first honest conversation either side has ever had.
about_author: Oscar Okafor is a former maritime radio operator who spent eleven years on cargo routes between West African ports before turning to fiction. He writes about distance, translation, and the people who keep lonely signals alive.

chapters.title: The Long Route
chapters.summary: Beatrix pilots the relay hauler Vesper between silent colony worlds, translating routine fleet traffic. She hasn't dreamed in a human language in six years, and she likes it that way — invisibility is safety. POV: Beatrix. Emotional beat: competent loneliness, a woman who has made a virtue of distance.

chapters.title: Signal at Meridian Deep
chapters.summary: A garbled transmission from the colony at Meridian Deep arrives containing a phoneme pattern Beatrix's instruments can't classify — but her sleeping mind almost can. She logs it and moves on, uneasy. POV: Beatrix. Emotional beat: the first itch of a mystery she'd rather ignore.

chapters.title: The Children Who Dream Together
chapters.summary: At Meridian Deep, colony doctor Ilsa Reyes treats forty children who wake each night reciting the same syllables in unison. Beatrix recognizes the cadence from the garbled signal. POV: Beatrix, with Ilsa's clinical notes interleaved. Emotional beat: wonder curdling into fear.

chapters.title: What the Fleet Pays For
chapters.summary: Fleet liaison Captain Osei contacts Beatrix privately: he knows about the dream, and he wants it classified as a psychological outbreak. She realizes the fleet has heard this language before — and made it extinct once. POV: Beatrix. Emotional beat: betrayal, the dawning cost of her neutrality.

chapters.title: A Grammar of Grief
chapters.summary: Beatrix begins decoding the children's dream with Ilsa's help, working through the night in the colony clinic. The language has no word for 'enemy' — only 'the one who stopped listening.' POV: Beatrix. Emotional beat: intimacy growing between her and Ilsa, translator and healer.

chapters.title: Invisible No Longer
chapters.summary: Fleet security arrives at Meridian Deep to quarantine the children. Beatrix's old handler, Wren, is aboard — and knows exactly who Beatrix used to be before she went dark. POV: Beatrix. Emotional beat: the past catching up; invisibility was always a debt.

chapters.title: The Debt of Translation
chapters.summary: Flashback chapter: fifteen years ago, Beatrix translated the surrender ultimatum that ended the first contact war, and the dreams stopped that night. She has run the long route ever since to avoid remembering. POV: Beatrix, past and present braided. Emotional beat: guilt as the engine of exile.

chapters.title: Ilsa's Argument
chapters.summary: Ilsa refuses to hand over the children and forces Beatrix to choose a side for the first time in years. 'You keep saying you deliver messages. This one is addressed to you.' POV: Ilsa, then Beatrix. Emotional beat: love stated as a challenge, not a comfort.

chapters.title: The Dream in Full
chapters.summary: Beatrix dreams the message herself for the first time in six years — in the alien tongue, complete. It is not a warning or a weapon. It is an apology, offered by the species the fleet exterminated, for a war they believe they started. POV: Beatrix. Emotional beat: awe and vertigo; the message inverts everything.

chapters.title: Wren's Offer
chapters.summary: Wren offers Beatrix reinstatement, protection, and a quiet life — if she certifies the dream as noise. The fleet cannot afford the truth before the ceasefire vote. POV: Beatrix. Emotional beat: temptation of safety, the old exile whispering that silence is mercy.

chapters.title: Quarantine
chapters.summary: Fleet marines seal the clinic. Ilsa is detained for sedition; the children are sedated to stop the dreaming. Beatrix watches her translation equipment confiscated. POV: alternating Beatrix and Ilsa in detention. Emotional beat: despair, and the first spark of open defiance.

chapters.title: The Horizon Relay
chapters.summary: Beatrix remembers the horizon relay — an unlicensed transmitter on the system's edge she helped build in her invisible years, powerful enough to reach every world at once. Getting there means stealing her own ship back. POV: Beatrix. Emotional beat: resolve hardening into a plan.

chapters.title: Theft of the Vesper
chapters.summary: Beatrix hijacks the Vesper from the fleet dockyard with help from an unexpected ally: Wren, who cannot forgive the fleet but cannot report her either. A chase through the debris belts follows. POV: Beatrix, with Wren's conflicted log entries. Emotional beat: adrenaline and grief for a friendship that chose duty.

chapters.title: Children's Choir
chapters.summary: Before the Vesper clears the system, the sedated children wake at once and sing the message aloud across every open channel — the dream refusing to be suppressed. The fleet's own comms carry it now. POV: ensemble, anchored on Ilsa in detention hearing it. Emotional beat: the silenced speaking through the smallest voices.

chapters.title: What the Message Says
chapters.summary: Beatrix finishes the full translation in flight: the extinct civilization's apology, and a second part — coordinates of a surviving seed-vault, and a request to be answered, not avenged. Delivering it honestly could end the war; distorting it could start the next one. POV: Beatrix. Emotional beat: the weight of being the only honest channel left.

chapters.title: Intercept
chapters.summary: Osei's warship corners the Vesper at the system's edge. Osei, himself a colonist's son, reveals the fleet leadership knows the vault coordinates are real — and wants them seized as a war prize. POV: Osei, then Beatrix. Emotional beat: an antagonist revealed as a mirror; duty against duty.

chapters.title: The Choice at the Edge
chapters.summary: Beatrix must decide: broadcast the message whole and lose her translation gift — the relay burns out a translator's native dreaming to amplify — or distort it and keep herself intact. Ilsa's voice, smuggled over a prison channel, tells her she doesn't have to be the instrument. POV: Beatrix. Emotional beat: the novel's moral hinge, love against duty.

chapters.title: Broadcast
chapters.summary: Beatrix transmits the message unaltered to every world, colony and fleet alike, feeding the relay her own human dreaming as fuel. The last human language she dreams in is the one the children sang. POV: Beatrix. Emotional beat: sacrifice as translation — giving up her self to carry someone else's voice.

chapters.title: Ceasefire at Meridian Deep
chapters.summary: The ceasefire vote collapses — not into war, but into something unprecedented: both fleets demand to answer the message directly. Osei stands down rather than fire on the relay. Wren testifies about the first war's cover-up. POV: ensemble. Emotional beat: relief that feels like falling; justice arriving outside any courtroom.

chapters.title: The Seed Vault
chapters.summary: A joint colony-fleet expedition reaches the vault and finds living members of the 'extinct' species, dormant and waiting. Beatrix, her gift spent, must teach others to translate — beginning with the children. POV: Beatrix and Ilsa. Emotional beat: humility; the translator becomes the student of her own students.

chapters.title: First Conversation
chapters.summary: The first true dialogue between humanity and the vault survivors is conducted by the dream-children, with Beatrix listening. The apology is finally answered in kind. POV: Beatrix, mostly silent for the first time in the book. Emotional beat: peace as an ongoing act of listening, not a signed document.

chapters.title: Mirabel and the Horizon
chapters.summary: Months later, Beatrix — dreaming again, in a language that is newly, jointly human and otherwise — chooses to stay at Meridian Deep with Ilsa rather than run the long route. The horizon is no longer something she flees toward. POV: Beatrix. Emotional beat: arrival; identity no longer defined by exile, love no longer at war with duty.
